books.section: Topic 5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: General Robert E. Lee, General Order No. 9 (April 10, 1865)

stimulus.source_note: General Robert E. Lee, General Order No. 9, April 10, 1865. Public domain. “. . .” marks omitted text.
stimulus.text:
“After four years of arduous service marked by unsurpassed courage and fortitude, the Army of Northern Virginia has been compelled to yield to overwhelming numbers and resources. . . . I need not tell the survivors of so many hard-fought battles, who have remained steadfast to the last, that I have consented to the result from no distrust of them.”

—General Robert E. Lee, General Order No. 9 (Farewell Address), April 10, 1865

rationales.A: Lee praises his men’s courage and says he does not distrust them.
rationales.B: Lee names the cause plainly: overwhelming numbers and resources on the Union side.
rationales.C: Lee says his men showed unsurpassed courage and fortitude.
rationales.D: Background: no foreign power intervened. Lee names numbers and resources, not Europe.
rationales.general:
1. Lee names two things, and only two: numbers and resources.
2. Numbers means men, and resources means supplies, guns, food, and railroads.
3. He does not blame his soldiers, his generals, or any foreign power.
4. The sentence is an epitaph for the Confederacy’s arithmetic: too few men, too little to fight with.
Remember: when a loser names the cause, take the nouns seriously: numbers and resources.
